old_entry.summary: Satoru Iwata is born in Sapporo on December 6, 1959, becoming a programmer, executive and president of Nintendo from 2002 to 2015.
body: Satoru Iwata is born in Sapporo on December 6, 1959, becoming a programmer, executive and president of Nintendo from 2002 to 2015. He is often remembered for the direct tone with which he spoke to the public, but the most interesting part of his career lies in the continuity among code, organization and communication. Before leading Nintendo, he worked for many years at HAL Laboratory, contributing to technically complex projects and learning to read development problems from the inside. As president, he defended an idea of innovation that did not coincide with hardware power alone: Nintendo DS and Wii sought new gestures, new audiences and new occasions for play. With Iwata Asks, he also turned the production process into editorial material, letting programmers, designers and technicians speak with unusual precision for the industry.

Iwata's career begins far from boardrooms. At HAL Laboratory he works as a programmer in an era when memory, performance and development tools impose severe limits. That technical training remains central even when he takes on managerial roles. In Nintendo's accounts of Balloon Fight, for example, he is remembered as responsible for programming the NES version. It is not an ornamental biographical detail: it means the future president directly understood the cost of a design choice, the fragility of a system and the work required to make an idea stable. His ability to speak with developers grows from this shared vocabulary built through code. Later, that background allows him to mediate among creative ambition, technical constraints and commercial needs without treating them as separate worlds.

One of the most revealing stories concerns Pokémon. When Game Freak was already busy with Pokémon Gold and Silver, Iwata found himself acting as a link between Nintendo and the team to address the Western localization of Pokémon Red and Green. In the Iwata Asks series, he explains that he obtained the source code and studied it to suggest how the work could be organized. The episode shows his method better than many abstract definitions: before imposing a solution, he tried to understand the existing system and the reasons it had become difficult to modify. It is a form of technical leadership based on analysis rather than the prestige of the role. Even as an executive, he would continue to regard understanding the process as a condition for making decisions, maintaining an unusual relationship between corporate responsibility and concrete development practice.

Iwata does not jump suddenly from programming to the presidency of Nintendo. He first leads HAL Laboratory, the studio where he had built much of his professional identity. That transition forces him to deal not only with software, but with people, deadlines, priorities and the sustainability of the company. In later conversations with Kirby developers, he often returns to that period as someone who knows HAL's culture from the inside and understands the difficulty of bringing a project to completion. It is significant that years later he can sit across from former colleagues and openly discuss canceled games, failed attempts and organizational decisions. The lesson is that production is not an administrative backdrop: it is part of design. A game exists only if the group can turn different skills into a process stable enough to reach the public.

As president, Iwata supports a strategy that rejects competition reduced to computing power. Nintendo DS and Wii instead ask which gestures can become immediately understandable and which people can feel invited to play. The dual screens, touch screen, motion-sensitive remote and readable home interface are industrial choices, but also hypotheses about the audience. They do not eliminate the complexity of video games; they redistribute it. Part of the work moves from the player to the device, from learning abstract combinations to recognizing familiar actions. This direction does not come from a single game and does not produce uniform results, but it changes how Nintendo defines innovation. For Iwata, technology is useful when it creates a new relationship between people and software, not when it remains confined to a specification sheet.

With Iwata Asks, Nintendo's president takes on an editorial role unusual for an executive at that level. The conversations do not merely promote a product: they reconstruct prototypes, failures, compromises, tools and relationships among departments. Iwata can ask technical questions because he recognizes the language of the people he is speaking with, but above all he leaves room for their answers. The result is a public archive of the work normally invisible behind a video game. Even when the tone is light, details emerge about who proposed a feature, why a version was abandoned or how a hardware constraint changed the project. This form of communication changes the relationship between company and public: the finished product is not presented as an object that appeared suddenly, but as the result of a collective history made of attempts, corrections and shared responsibilities.

Iwata's communication becomes memorable because it retains something of the way a programmer reasons. In presentations and interviews, he tends to break down a problem, explain the context and show who worked on the solution. This approach helps humanize Nintendo without turning the executive into a simple advertising face. The historical value of his figure also lies here: he makes visible that a large video game company is made of technical, creative and organizational decisions that can be explained clearly. After his death in 2015, Nintendo officially documented his career and date of birth, but the most concrete legacy remains in the processes and archives he helped make public. His idea of leadership does not erase the distance between company and audience, but tries to make its steps understandable.

editorial_features.title: Ask where the decision came from
body: In the Wii Remote interview, Satoru Iwata asks Genyo Takeda what preceded the finished controller. Takeda describes small teams pairing GameCube software with dedicated interfaces, including the work that produced the Donkey Konga bongos and a dance mat. Another participant, Ikeda, traces his sensor experience through Pocket Pikachu and Kirby Tilt 'n' Tumble. The question turns a familiar object into a sequence of experiments by named people. A visitor can see that the controller did not arrive complete from a single instruction issued at the top.

Iwata then asks industrial designer Kenichiro Ashida about a turning point. Ashida explains the distance between his experience as a creator and as a parent with less time to play demanding games. Simply adding functions to another two-handed controller no longer answered that problem for him. The exchange preserves an individual reason inside a corporate product. Iwata's role here is also editorial: he asks for the change in thinking, rather than treating the final remote's unusual shape as sufficient explanation of how it came to exist.

The Wii Fit conversation exposes mistaken simplicity. Iwata asks when measuring balance entered the project, and hears two routes: hardware planners considered sumo wrestlers using two scales; a software developer found a posture method using a similar arrangement. Comparable prototypes did not require identical origins. The conversation then reaches rejected proposals and a team close to giving up. A product is easier to understand when its participants can describe uncertainty and disagreement without pretending that everyone recognised the answer from the beginning.

Later in that exchange, the board's width becomes the issue. Developers had concentrated on keeping a bathroom-scale-sized device compact and inexpensive, until exercise footage made a shoulder-width stance obvious. Iwata asks how the team experienced this change, even while Miyamoto sits in the room. The discussion allows conflicting instructions and practical frustration to remain visible. It is still a company-produced account, not an independent investigation. Its value lies in the explanation it preserves: the body, the budget and the size of an object were being negotiated together.

old_entry.title: The console that left room for a computer
old_entry.summary: Smith helped connect a game console to another household possibility.
body: In his Computer History Museum interview, Ed Smith began with appliances in Brownsville, Brooklyn. A repaired toaster led to other jobs, and word spread that he could make broken things work. He remembered reading, finding replacement parts and wanting to understand the electrical behaviour he encountered. This was technical learning grounded in actual objects, before he joined the team at APF. His account does not need an imposed destiny. It gives a sequence: curiosity became useful work, and useful work made a career in electronics seem possible.

At APF, Smith helped develop the MP 1000 console and the expansion that became the Imagination Machine. Benj Edwards’s published interview places him within a small engineering team, rather than describing the system as the work of one person. The possibility of expansion changes how we read the console. It could be a self-contained machine for running games, but it also formed the base of a different household computer. Smith’s story makes that junction visible. The history of home gaming included products that crossed categories instead of fitting neatly into the console or personal-computer shelf.

Smith’s own account describes the MPA-10 module joining the console to a keyboard, BASIC and a cassette recorder. Cassette material could combine program data with recorded speech, introducing software while it loaded. The controls and connections were therefore part of a proposal about what the buyer might do next. A game machine could become something to type on, learn from or program. The expansion did not erase the console beneath it. It extended an existing arrangement, using the capacity and interfaces of that machine to offer another kind of participation.

Later, Smith received requests to explain his APF work. In the 2020 oral history, he connected those inquiries with his decision to write Imagine That! The account is not a substitute for contemporary schematics or team records, but it supplies a named participant who can describe his work and question what has been omitted. A commercial ranking leaves little room for the Imagination Machine beside better-selling systems. Smith’s decision to record his experience gives the museum another measure: the knowledge of someone who helped make it.

old_entry.title: Trek-80
old_entry.summary: Trek-80 is a text-based video game written by Steve Dompier in 1976 and sold by Processor Technology for their Sol-20 computer and suitable S-100 bus machines.
body: Trek-80 is a text-based video game written by Steve Dompier in 1976 and sold by Processor Technology for their Sol-20 computer and suitable S-100 bus machines.

Trek-80 combines features of the seminal Star Trek game by Mike Mayfield with the unrelated Trek73. In contrast to the originals, which were designed to run on teletypes, Trek-80 used the VDM-1 video card to produce a character-based real-time display.
Compatible 3rd party versions of the VDM-1 became the de facto display for most early S-100 bus machines, as well as the TRS-80. A version known as Invasion Force was sold by Tandy for the TRS-80.
An unrelated Trek-80 for the TRS-80 was sold by Judges Guild, but this was a port of the original Mayfield game with few changes.

old_entry.title: Target
old_entry.summary: Target, or TARG, was an action video game written by Steve Dompier for the VDM-1 video card for S-100 bus microcomputers.
body: Target, or TARG, was an action video game written by Steve Dompier for the VDM-1 video card for S-100 bus microcomputers. It is among the earliest computer video games, released some time in 1976 or 1977.

The game used the VDM-1's graphics characters in a game that Dompier described as a "shoot the airplanes sort of game". The player had a gun that could be rotated left and right, firing at targets moving sideways across the top of the screen.

Target is almost certainly the first microcomputer game to be shown on national television. It appeared in late 1976 on The Tomorrow Show, mesmerizing the host Tom Snyder to the point where he had to be forced to stop playing it in order to finish the episode.
